Apple identifies these causes of quarterly net-sales fluctuations:

- **Seasonality:** First-quarter sales have historically been higher, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Launch timing can affect sales. In indirect channels, inventory of an older product often declines before a launch, while channels fill with new inventory afterward. Consumer and distributor anticipation can also affect sales.
- **Demand changes:** A significant portion of sales comes from a single product, so declining demand for it could substantially affect quarterly sales. Demand for products or services can also be lower than anticipated.
- **Unexpected disruptions:** These include problems with new introductions, IT system failures or network disruptions, and failures of logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners.

*Source: Apple fiscal 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 4 and 15.*

## Financial results

- **Exchange gain:** JPMorgan recorded an initial gain of **$7.990 billion** on May 6, based on the fair value of the Class C shares received. Note 2 rounds this to $8.0 billion. Subsequent second-quarter fair-value changes in the Class C shares and derivatives, plus dividends, resulted in a **$7.9 billion net Visa-related gain** in other income. The initial and net gains are not additive. (Form 10-K, pp. 200, 228)
- **Foundation contribution:** The Firm contributed **$1.0 billion** of Class C shares to its Foundation in the second quarter, recording the amount as noninterest expense. Combining that expense with the rounded $7.9 billion quarterly gain implies approximately **$6.9 billion of second-quarter pretax benefit**, before any later Visa-related effects. The remaining Class C shares were sold in the second and third quarters. (pp. 62, 200, 228)
- **Cash-flow reconciliation:** The statement of cash flows subtracts the **$7.990 billion** initial exchange gain from net income when reconciling operating cash flow. This is a reconciliation adjustment, not a second loss. (p. 176)
- **Taxes:** The Firm cited the Visa gain and contribution as part of the income-and-expense mix contributing to a higher effective tax rate: **22.1% in 2024 versus 19.6% in 2023**. It did not isolate a Visa-specific tax amount or rate effect. (p. 62)

The Class C position elevated the **average and maximum** Corporate, Other and firmwide Risk Management value-at-risk (VaR). The second-quarter rise and subsequent decline in daily VaR were primarily driven by changes in the Class C exposure. The measure uses an approximately 95% confidence level and a one-day holding period. (pp. 143–144)

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Corporate | 23 | 12 | 102 | 17 |

| Firmwide total | 47 | 43 | 91 | 57 |

The **$4 million increase in average firmwide VaR** was not attributed solely to Visa: purchased credit protection also contributed, partly offset by fixed-income volatility rolling out of the historical look-back period. The filing does not give a Visa-only VaR amount. (p. 144)
